units.title: Relief in Eritrea
units.intro: This unit is about the **relief** of Eritrea: the highlands, the escarpments and the lowlands. Eritrea has great physical diversity.

relief.title: The three relief divisions of Eritrea

altitude.title: From the lowest to the highest place

profile.title: A walk from west to east (cross-section)

cards.title: Relief
body: **Relief** means the shape of the earth's surface.
In Eritrea the land is not the same everywhere. Eritrea has physical variations (differences).

cards.title: Low and high places
body: Move the slider. See the **altitude** (height) of each place.

states.label: Lowest
states.text: The **Danakil Depression**: about 120 metres **below** sea level.

states.label: Sea level
states.text: Sea level is 0 metres. The Red Sea coast is near sea level.

states.label: 1500 m
states.text: Land higher than 1500 metres is called **highland** in Eritrea.

states.label: Highest
states.text: **Mount Soira**: over 3000 metres above sea level. It is the highest point.

cards.title: What is a depression?
body: A **depression** is a hollow (sunken) area. Higher land is all around it.
A depression has no outlet for surface water.
So when it rains, the water of the streams stays inside the depression.

cards.title: Why is relief important?
body: Differences in relief cause differences in:
- climate, natural vegetation, soil and wild animals.
Relief also changes where people live and work:
- population, settlement, economic activities and transportation.

cards.title: Three relief divisions
body: Eritrea has three broad relief divisions. They are based on altitude.
They are the **highlands**, the **escarpments** and the **lowlands**. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Memory trick: the three divisions
body: Think **H-E-L**: go from the **H**igh land, down the **E**scarpment, to the **L**ow land.

cards.q: Eritrea is divided into three relief divisions based on:
cards.why: The textbook says the three broad relief divisions are based on altitude.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Relief = shape of the earth's surface.
Lowest: Danakil Depression (about 120 m below sea level).
Highest: Mount Soira (over 3000 m).

cards.title: What is a highland?
body: In Eritrea, land higher than **1500 metres** above sea level is called **highland**.
The highlands are in the central part of the country.
They go from the Ethiopia border in the south to the Sudan border in the north.

cards.title: Broad in the south, narrow in the north
body: Move the slider to see each division.

states.label: Highlands
states.text: The highlands are much **broader in the south**. They become narrower towards the north. Their altitude also goes down from south to north.

states.label: Escarpments
states.text: The escarpments are between the highlands and the lowlands.

states.label: East low
states.text: The Eastern Lowlands are between the Eastern Escarpment and the Red Sea.

states.label: West low
states.text: The Western Lowlands are in the western and north-western parts.

cards.title: The highest mountains
body: The highest altitudes are on the **eastern edge** of the highlands, near the Eastern Escarpment.
The highest mountains are **Mount Soira**, **Mount Aba Hani**, **Mount Tarika**, **Mount Metera** and **Mount Saim**.

cards.title: Memory trick: highest mountains
body: **Some Apples Taste Much Sweeter**. Soira comes first: it is the highest.

cards.title: Plateaus and rivers
body: The highlands are **flat at the top**. They form wide **plateaus**.
Most rivers in Eritrea start in the highlands.
These rivers have cut deep **gorges**. Examples: Haddas Gorge, Felket Gorge, Labka Gorge and Anseba Gorge.

cards.title: Gorge, trough, depression
body: Move the slider. Compare the three shapes.

states.label: Gorge
states.text: A **gorge** is a deep, narrow valley with steep sides.

states.label: Trough
states.text: A **trough** is a deep, long, U-shaped valley. The river in a trough has an outlet: the water can flow out.

states.label: Depression
states.text: A **depression** also looks low and hollow, but it has **no outlet**. The water stays inside.

cards.title: Troughs in the highlands
body: There are troughs inside the highlands. Examples:
- Keren Trough
- Hazemo Trough
- Agrae Trough (near Nakfa)

cards.title: Do not mix them up
head: Shape
Outlet?
rows: yes, the river has an outlet

cards.q: Which one has NO outlet for its water?
cards.why: A depression is enclosed by higher land. Water stays inside. The rivers in troughs have outlets.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Highlands: over 1500 m, centre of Eritrea, south to north.
Broad in the south, narrow in the north.
Flat tops = plateaus. Most rivers start here.

cards.title: What is an escarpment?
body: An **escarpment** is a long steep slope or cliff.
It separates high ground (a plateau) from the plain below.
In Eritrea the escarpments are between the highlands and the lowlands. They are rugged and very steep.

steps.text: Start in the **Western Lowlands**. The land is low.
Climb the **Western Escarpment**. It faces the Western Lowlands.
Now you are on the flat **highland plateau**. A river has cut a deep **gorge**.
Go down the **Eastern Escarpment**. It faces the Eastern Lowlands and the Red Sea.
Cross the dry **Eastern Lowlands**.
You reach the **Red Sea** coast.

cards.title: Escarpments change towards the north
body: Towards the north the escarpments become **narrower**.
They also become lower. They change into gentle slopes.
There are two escarpments: the **Eastern Escarpment** and the **Western Escarpment**.

cards.title: The Eastern Escarpment
body: It is the slope facing the Eastern Lowlands and the Red Sea. Examples:
- the slope between Betghiorghis (Asmara) and Sabarguma
- Semenawi Bahri and Debubawi Bahri
- Nefasit, Imbatkala, Ghindae and Dongolo

cards.title: The Western Escarpment
body: It is the slope facing the Western Lowlands. Examples:
- all slopes facing Mensura, Hagaz and Sawa
- in the Southern Region: slopes facing Mai Duma and Hazemo, and the slope south of Adi Quala

cards.q: Ghindae and Nefasit are on the:
cards.why: The textbook lists Nefasit, Imbatkala, Ghindae and Dongolo along the Eastern Escarpment.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Eastern Escarpment faces the Red Sea (East = sEa).
Western Escarpment faces the Western Lowlands.
Both are steep. Both get narrower to the north.

cards.title: What are lowlands?
body: **Lowlands** are areas below 1500 metres above sea level.
Some places in the lowlands are even below sea level.
They are east and west of the highlands: the **Eastern Lowlands** and the **Western Lowlands**.

cards.title: The Eastern Lowlands
body: This is the land between the Eastern Escarpment and the Red Sea coast.
It goes from **Karora** (Sudan border) in the north to the **Djibouti** border in the south.
Its altitude goes from below sea level to over 700 metres near the highlands.

cards.title: The Danakil Depression
body: The **Danakil Depression** is south of the Gulf of Zula, in the Eastern Lowlands.
Its altitude is below sea level.
Some lakes in the Danakil Depression are about 120 metres below sea level.

cards.title: Volcanoes and a block mountain
body: The Eastern Lowlands have some volcanic mountains and block mountains.
Some volcanoes are **active volcanoes**. Tap the dots to find them.

cards.title: Five active volcanoes
body: - Mount **Dubbi**, south of Edi
- Mount **Alid**, south of Irafale
- Mount **Dollah**, in the Buri Peninsula
- Mount **Arta-ale**, south of Bada
- Mount **Kusurale**, near Irafale
Mount **Ghedem** is an example of a **block mountain**.

cards.title: Memory trick: active volcanoes
body: **Dad Asks: Danger? Active Kettles!** A volcano is like a hot kettle.
And G for Ghedem = a block (not a volcano).

cards.title: How does a hot spring form?

steps.text: Rain water seeps down into the ground. It becomes groundwater.
Deep in the ground the water touches **hot rocks**. The water becomes hot.
When the amount of groundwater increases, the hot water rises.
It flows out onto the surface. This is a **hot spring**. People bathe in it.

cards.title: Hot springs in the Eastern Lowlands
body: Examples of hot springs: Ailet (in Gahtelay), Felhit (north of Geleb), Irafale, Mount Kusurale and Hasmet.
People believe hot springs have medicinal value.
They bathe in them to be cured of some muscle and breathing (respiratory) diseases.

cards.title: Rivers cross the dry east
body: The Eastern Lowlands are dry. But several rivers from the highlands cross them.
Examples: **Haddas**, **Laba**, **Labka**, **Felket**, **Comayle** and **Alighede**.

cards.q: Mount Ghedem is an example of:
cards.why: The textbook says Mount Ghedem is an example of a block mountain.

cards.title: The Western Lowlands
body: They are the western and north-western parts of Eritrea.
Molki, Mai Duma and southern Hazemo are also parts (extensions) of the Western Lowlands.
Places: Hagaz, Akurdet, Tessenei, Om-Hager and Sawa.
Near the Barka River, close to the Sudan border, the altitude is below 500 metres.

cards.title: North-west or south-west?
head: North-west
South-west
rows: people moved with animals to find pasture and water
rich in grass and wild animals, fertile soil
sorghum, pearl millet; sesame, cotton, vegetables, fruits

cards.title: Plains and big rivers
body: The lowlands have broad plains, small hills and some isolated mountains.
**Mereb (Gash)**, **Barka** and **Anseba** rivers cross the Western Lowlands.
These rivers have a very great potential for irrigation farming.

cards.q: Which river crosses the Western Lowlands?
cards.why: Mereb (Gash), Barka and Anseba cross the Western Lowlands. Felket, Labka and Haddas cross the Eastern Lowlands.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Lowlands: below 1500 m, east and west of the highlands.
East: Danakil Depression, active volcanoes, hot springs.
West: Mereb (Gash), Barka, Anseba; dry north-west, wet south-west.

highland that is flat at the top
a steep-sided, deep and narrow valley

a type of mountain; Mount Ghedem is an example

tips.text: Learn the numbers: **1500 m** (highland line), **over 3000 m** (Mount Soira), **about 120 m below sea level** (Danakil lakes), **over 700 m** (top of the Eastern Lowlands), **below 500 m** (near the Barka River).
When a question asks about a place, first decide: **east or west?** East = Red Sea side (Haddas, Felket, Labka, volcanoes, hot springs). West = Sudan side (Mereb-Gash, Barka, Anseba, Tessenei, Sawa).
Definition words to know exactly: relief, depression, gorge, trough, escarpment, hot spring. Say each one in one short sentence.
"All are correct" is often the right answer when the textbook gives a list, for example: relief differences cause variation of climate, soil **and** wild animals.

cards.back: The shape of the earth's surface.
A hollow, sunken area with higher land around it. No outlet.
A steep-sided, deep, narrow valley.
A deep, long, U-shaped valley. Its river has an outlet.
A long steep slope or cliff between a plateau and the plain below.
Heated groundwater that flows out onto the surface.
Example: Mount Ghedem.
Height above sea level. Eritrea: from about 120 m below sea level to over 3000 m.

questions.q: The shape of the earth's surface is called:
why: **Relief** means the shape of the earth's surface.
Altitude is height. A depression and a plateau are kinds of landforms.
questions.tip: Relief = shape. Altitude = height.

similar.q: Height above sea level is called ___.

questions.q: The highest point of Eritrea is:
why: The textbook says the altitude goes up to over 3000 metres at **Mount Soira**.
Aba Hani, Metera and Tarika are high, but Soira is the highest.
questions.tip: In the trick "Some Apples Taste Much Sweeter", S for Soira comes first because it is the highest.

similar.q: Where is the lowest point of Eritrea?

questions.q: Differences in relief in Eritrea have caused variation of:
why: Relief differences caused variation of climate, natural vegetation, soil and wild animals.
So all three choices are correct.
questions.tip: If every choice is in the textbook list, choose "all".

similar.q: Name two human things that relief influences.
similar.a: Any two: population, settlement, economic activities, transportation.

questions.q: A hollow or sunken area with higher land around it and no outlet is a:
why: A **depression** is sunken and enclosed by higher land.
It has no outlet, so rain water stays inside.
A trough looks similar but its river has an outlet.
questions.tip: No way out = depression.

similar.q: Give an example of a trough in Eritrea.
similar.a: Keren Trough (also Hazemo or Agrae Trough).

questions.q: In Eritrea, land with an altitude greater than ___ metres is called highland.
why: The textbook says land higher than 1500 metres above sea level is highland.
Lowlands are below 1500 metres.
questions.tip: 1500 is the line between high and low.

similar.q: Lowlands in Eritrea are areas below ___ metres.

questions.q: The highlands of Eritrea are broader in the north than in the south.
why: The highlands are much **broader in the south**.
They become narrower and narrower towards the north.
questions.tip: South = broad; North = narrow (and lower).

similar.q: True or false: the altitude of the highlands decreases from south to north.

questions.q: Highlands which are flat at the top are called:
why: The highlands are flat at the top and form extensive **plateaus**.
questions.tip: Plateau = a high, flat table of land.

similar.q: Most rivers in Eritrea start from the ___.

questions.q: Deep, steep-sided and narrow valleys are called ___.
why: Gorges are steep-sided, deep and narrow valleys.
Examples: Haddas, Felket, Labka and Anseba gorges.
questions.tip: Gorge = narrow like a V. Trough = wide like a U.

similar.q: Name one gorge in Eritrea.
similar.a: Haddas Gorge (or Felket, Labka, Anseba Gorge).

questions.q: Which of the following is a trough?
why: The textbook gives Keren Trough, Hazemo Trough and Agrae Trough.
Danakil is a depression. Semenawi Bahri is on the Eastern Escarpment.
questions.tip: Troughs: K-H-A = Keren, Hazemo, Agrae.

similar.q: Agrae Trough is near which town?

questions.q: The steep slopes between the highlands and the lowlands are called what? Name the two.
questions.answer: Escarpments: the Eastern Escarpment and the Western Escarpment.
why: An escarpment is a long steep slope between a plateau and the plain below.
The Eastern one faces the Red Sea; the Western one faces the Western Lowlands.
questions.tip: Name both: East and West.

similar.q: Which escarpment faces Hagaz and Sawa?

questions.q: Which is an active volcano in Eritrea?
why: The active volcanoes are Dubbi, Alid, Dollah, Arta-ale and Kusurale.
So A, B and C are all correct.
questions.tip: Remember "Dad Asks: Danger? Active Kettles!" (Dubbi, Alid, Dollah, Arta-ale, Kusurale).

similar.q: An example of a block mountain in Eritrea is ___.

questions.q: Why do people bathe in hot springs?
questions.answer: They believe hot springs have medicinal value; they bathe to be cured of some muscle, respiratory and other diseases.
why: The textbook says people believe hot springs have medicinal values.
They bathe in them to get cured of some muscular and respiratory diseases.
questions.tip: Hot spring = believed to heal (medicine).

similar.q: Name two hot springs in the Eastern Lowlands.
similar.a: Any two: Ailet (Gahtelay), Felhit, Irafale, Mount Kusurale, Hasmet.

questions.q: Which area is below sea level?
why: The Danakil Depression is below sea level; some lakes there are about 120 m below sea level.
Hazemo, Sawa and Tessenei are above sea level.
questions.tip: Below sea level = Danakil.

similar.q: The Eastern Lowlands go from Karora in the north to the ___ border in the south.

questions.q: The south-western part of the Western Lowlands is wet, rich in grass and has fertile soil.
why: The textbook says the south-western part is wet and rich in grass and wild animals, with fertile soil.
The north-western part is very dry.
questions.tip: South-west = wet. North-west = dry.

similar.q: Name two crops of the south-western lowlands.
similar.a: Any two: sorghum, pearl millet, sesame, cotton, vegetables, fruits.

units.title: Hydrology and River System in Eritrea
units.intro: This unit is about water: the water cycle, rivers, lakes, the Red Sea, groundwater, and why there is a shortage of water in Eritrea.

gw.title: Groundwater in the rainy and dry seasons

cards.title: Where does rain water go?
body: Some rain water **seeps** down into the ground. This forms **groundwater**. Springs and wells get their water from groundwater.
Some rain water flows on the surface. This forms rivers and streams.
Rivers and streams flow into oceans, seas or lakes.

cards.title: Evaporation and transpiration
body: **Evaporation**: water changes into vapour from rivers, lakes, ponds, seas and oceans, because of high temperature.
**Transpiration**: on hot days, plants give out water vapour through tiny holes in their leaves. These holes are called **stomata**.
**Evapo-transpiration** = evaporation + transpiration together (loss of moisture).

cards.title: The water cycle, step by step

steps.text: The sun heats the sea. Water changes into vapour: **evaporation**.
Plants give out water vapour from their leaves: **transpiration**.
The water vapour rises. It cools and changes into water droplets. The droplets form **clouds**.
We get **rain** from the clouds. Most rain falls on the highlands.
Some rain water flows in rivers back to the sea.
Some rain water seeps into the ground and forms **groundwater**. Then the cycle starts again.

cards.title: Hydrologic cycle and hydrology
body: The **hydrologic cycle** (water cycle) is a continuous process. Water moves from the earth's surface to the atmosphere and back again.
**Hydrology** is a science about the waters of the earth (surface water and groundwater):
- their distribution
- their chemical and physical properties
- the water cycle

cards.q: Plants give out water vapour through stomata. This is called:
cards.why: Transpiration is when plants release water vapour through the tiny holes (stomata) in their leaves.

cards.title: Parts of a river system
body: All the water in rivers, lakes and seas comes from rain. Tap the dots to learn the parts of a river.

cards.title: River words
head: Word
Meaning
rows: the place where a river starts (wet highland, lakes or snow areas)
the place where a river ends (a lake, sea or ocean)
a small river that joins the main river
the place where a small river joins the main river

cards.title: Memory trick: river words
body: A river is like a person. It is born at the **Source**. It gets a **Tiny friend** (tributary). They **Come together** (confluence). It ends at the **Mouth**.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Evaporation = from water bodies. Transpiration = from plants.
Water cycle = water goes up and comes down again and again.
Hydrology = the science of the earth's waters.

cards.title: Surface water
body: **Surface water** includes rivers, ponds, reservoirs, lakes, seas and oceans.
The amount of water in them depends on the amount of **rainfall**.
Where rain is small and seasonal, rivers are seasonal too.
Where rain is heavy all year, rivers flow all year. They are **permanent rivers**, for example River Zaire.

cards.title: No permanent rivers in Eritrea
body: Rainfall in Eritrea is low and irregular. Droughts are common. Evaporation is high.
So there are **no permanent rivers** in Eritrea. Rivers have water only in the rainy seasons.
The highlands are wetter than the lowlands. So most rivers start in the highlands.

cards.title: Rivers of Eritrea
body: Tap the dots to see the names. The yellow star is Asmara.

cards.title: Mereb (Gash) River
body: The **largest and longest** river in Eritrea.
Its source is Mount (Emba) Tekera, south-east of Asmara.
It has a curved course. It passes close to Dubarwa and reaches Hazemo. Then it turns west.
In Gash-Barka Region it is called **Gash**. Finally it enters the Sudan.

cards.title: Barka and Anseba Rivers
body: **Barka** starts near Mai Nefhi, west of Asmara. Its upper part is called **Mensura** River. It crosses the Western Escarpment, passes close to Akurdet and turns north.
**Anseba** starts from Asmara. It flows straight to Keren, then north-west. It joins the Zara River at Sher-it.
Anseba joins Barka at Sala. Then they enter the Sudan.

cards.title: Haddas and Alighede Rivers
body: **Haddas** starts near Adi Keih. It cuts the Eastern Escarpment into a deep gorge.
**Alighede** collects water from Ala, Mai Habar and Bet Ghiorgis of Asmara.
Haddas and Alighede meet at **Wia**, near Foro. Wia has a lot of groundwater.
Wia is a Saho word. It means **flooding**.

cards.title: Felket, Labka, Dandero and Indeli
body: **Felket** starts in the mountains north-east of Nakfa. It flows through the Agrae Trough and enters the Red Sea at **Mersa Teklay**.
**Labka** starts near Geleb. It enters the Red Sea at **Marsa Kubae**.
**Dandero** starts on the plateau of Soira and drains into Sumoti (Danakil Depression).
**Indeli** starts south of Senafe. It enters the Bada Depression, where it is used for irrigation.

cards.title: Where do the rivers go?
body: The rivers radiate (spread out) from the highlands. Move the slider.

states.label: Sudan
states.text: Most **large** rivers flow into the **Sudan**: Mereb (Gash), Barka and Anseba.

states.label: Red Sea
states.text: Rivers to the **Red Sea**: Felket, Laba, Labka, Haddas and Alighede.

states.label: Danakil
states.text: Rivers to the **Danakil Depression**: Dandero and Indeli.

cards.title: Memory trick: rivers to the Sudan
body: **My Big Adventure** goes west to the Sudan. The three big rivers all start near Asmara.

cards.title: Gorges cut by rivers
body: Mereb-Gash, Barka, Anseba and Alighede start near Asmara. Haddas starts near Adi Keih.
Many rivers have cut the plateaus and escarpments into deep gorges.
Examples: Aget Gorge, Felket Gorge, Haddas Gorge, Labka Gorge.

cards.q: The river whose source is Mount Tekera is:
cards.why: The textbook says the source of the Mereb River is Mount (Emba) Tekera, south-east of Asmara.

cards.title: Lakes
body: Rainfall is low and unreliable. So Eritrea has **no significant natural lakes**.
The few lakes are in the Eastern Lowlands, south of the Gulf of Zula:
- crater lakes at Mount Abihe Bad and Abihe Bet (extinct volcanoes)
- Lake Bada and Lake Aba Adad (Danakil Depression)
- Lake Bordele (Buri Peninsula)

cards.title: Ponds and dams
body: Since independence many ponds and dams have been built. They are **artificial lakes**.
Why? To conserve soil and water, and to use the water for drinking and irrigation.
The largest dams are **Toker**, **Gerset** and **Mai Nefhi**.
Toker and Mai Nefhi give water to Asmara. Gerset is south of Tessenei; it is used for irrigation.

cards.title: The Eritrean Red Sea
body: The central part of the Red Sea is an international sea.
Eritrean marine water and islands cover more than **121,000 km²** of the 456,000 km² of the Red Sea.
The widest part of the Red Sea is between Eritrea and Saudi Arabia: about **300 km**.

cards.title: The continental shelf
body: A **continental shelf** is a gently sloping, shallow sea bed next to a continent.
In Eritrea it is widest at Massawa: up to **120 km** from the coast.
In the north and south it is only about 20 km wide. It is about 182 metres deep.

cards.title: A salty sea
body: The Red Sea water has a high concentration of salt. Three reasons:
- no permanent rivers flow into it
- low rainfall
- high evaporation
The Dead Sea (between Israel and Jordan) has the highest concentration of salt in the world.

cards.title: Rich sea life
body: The Eritrean Red Sea is rich in marine biodiversity.
At least **17%** of its 1400 fish species and **20%** of its 250 coral fish species live nowhere else in the world.
It has coral reefs, mangrove, sea grass and sea weed.
Animals: turtles, dugongs, sea birds, dolphins and whales.

cards.title: Memory trick: why so salty?
body: **R-R-E**: no **R**ivers, little **R**ain, much **E**vaporation. Say: "Red Sea: R, R, E!"

cards.q: The widest part of the Red Sea is between:
cards.why: The widest part, about 300 km, is between Eritrea and Saudi Arabia.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: No permanent rivers: they flow only in the rainy season.
To the Sudan: Mereb-Gash, Barka, Anseba. To the Red Sea: Haddas, Felket, Labka. To the Danakil: Dandero, Indeli.
Largest dams: Toker, Gerset, Mai Nefhi.

cards.title: Rainy season and dry season
body: Move the slider. Watch the water in the well.

states.label: Rainy
states.text: In the rainy season the groundwater rises (water table 1). The well has water.

states.label: Dry
states.text: In the dry season the groundwater goes down (water table 2). The well has little water.

cards.title: Layers under the ground
body: Water seeps through **permeable** rock. It cannot pass through **impermeable** rock. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Groundwater comes from rain
body: Groundwater is formed from rainfall. More rain = more groundwater.
When it rains, some water evaporates, some is lost by transpiration, and some flows to rivers, lakes and ponds.
Some seeps into the ground. This forms groundwater.

cards.title: More or less groundwater?
head: Less groundwater
More groundwater
rows: impermeable rock: water cannot seep down

cards.title: Places rich in groundwater
body: Places with **alluvial soils** have a lot of groundwater. Large rivers cross them.
Examples: Hazemo Plains, Tessenei area, Alighider, Goluge, the Eastern Lowlands, and coastal places such as Wia and Wekiro.

cards.title: How deep is the groundwater?
head: Place
Depth
rows: Escarpments, Western Lowlands, banks of Anseba, Barka, Mereb-Gash, Setit; Damas, Ala, Mensura, Hazemo Plain

cards.title: Altitude and evapo-transpiration
body: Temperature controls evapo-transpiration. Temperature depends on altitude.
At sea level, evapo-transpiration is very high. It goes down as altitude goes up.
So it is low in the highlands but very high in the lowlands.

cards.q: Which kind of soil has a large amount of groundwater?
cards.why: Places with alluvial soils have a large amount of groundwater. Limestone and sandstone do not let water seep down.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Rainy season: water table high. Dry season: water table low.
Trees, grass and alluvial soil = more groundwater.
Steep land, bare land, impermeable rock = less groundwater.

cards.title: Why is there a shortage?
body: There is a shortage of water in Eritrea. It is linked with **drought** and **low rainfall**.
Almost all rivers flow only in the rainy seasons. So rivers are not permanent sources of water for drinking and irrigation.
People build ponds, dams and wells. Some collect water from roofs in the rainy season.

cards.title: Floods and erosion
body: These cause **flooding**: steep slopes, impermeable rocks, poor vegetation cover and **torrential rainfall** (heavy rain for a short time).
Because of deforestation, most of Eritrea's soils are open to heavy erosion.
The eroded soil (silt) fills the dams. Clearing silt is difficult.

cards.title: A dam silting up
body: Move the slider: stage A, B, C.

states.label: A
states.text: Stage A: abundant (a lot of) water.

states.label: B
states.text: Stage B: silt has been deposited. The dam stores less water.

states.label: C
states.text: Stage C: so much silt that the water is reduced tremendously.

cards.title: Short-lived dams
body: Dams on the escarpments and lowlands are short-lived because of silt. Examples:
- Zula Dam at Foro
- Danadai Dam on River Mai Adkemom, near Ghindae
- the dams around the Elabered citrus plantation

cards.title: Memory trick: stop the silt
body: We still need dams. To stop them silting up, think **TARC**: Terrace, Afforest, Reforest, Check dams.

cards.title: Solutions to the shortage
body: - build dams and ponds
- divert rivers in the lowlands to grow crops
- conserve water: collect water from roofs
- plant trees and grass: less erosion (dams do not fill with silt) and more water seeps down (more groundwater)

cards.q: The main problem of dams and ponds in Eritrea is:
cards.why: Dams fill with silt within a short time because of high erosion linked with deforestation.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Causes of shortage: drought, low and unreliable rainfall, seasonal rain, high evapo-transpiration.
Deforestation → erosion → silt fills dams.
Solutions: dams, ponds, river diversion, roof water, trees and grass.

units.title: The Environment, People and Development
units.intro: This unit shows how Eritreans live in different environments, how people change the natural environment, the bad effects of these changes, and how to protect the environment.

tech.title: Simple and advanced technology in a hot, dry desert

defor.title: What happens when trees are cut?

pins.text: water lost from the soil by evaporation

cards.title: Natural resources
body: **Natural resources** are part of the physical environment. They are useful to people. They are formed naturally.
Examples: air, water, land, vegetation, soils, animals, plants and minerals.

cards.title: Using resources changes the land
body: When people take minerals like coal or iron from the earth:
- vegetation is cleared (deforestation)
- holes are dug
- roads are built to carry the minerals
- houses for miners and power stations are built
So the natural environment is changed (modified).

cards.title: Wealth = resources + technology
body: The wealth of a nation depends on its natural resources and its technology.
USA and Canada are rich in natural resources.
**Japan** is poor in natural resources. But it has advanced technology. It imports raw materials, manufactures them and exports the products.

cards.title: What is technology?
body: **Technology** is the knowledge, skills, tools and machines that people have.
People in the world have different levels of technology.
Technology changes the way natural resources are used.

cards.title: Bushmen and Arizona
body: Both live in hot, dry deserts. Move the slider.

states.label: Bushmen
states.text: The **Bushmen** live in the Kalahari Desert (southern Africa). Simple technology: bows, arrows, digging sticks. They hunt and collect fruits and roots. They change the environment very little.

states.label: Arizona
states.text: The people of **Arizona** (USA) have advanced technology. They built dams to irrigate the desert. It became green farmland. They built cities, air-conditioned buildings and piped water.

cards.title: New uses of resources
body: As technology improves, people find new uses for resources.
In the past, oil was used only as fuel for transport and energy.
Today oil is also a raw material for rubber tyres, detergents, paints, plastic basins, insecticides and asphalt.

cards.title: Development
body: **Development** means how far the natural resources of a country are brought into full production.
With advanced technology, the dry lowlands of Eritrea could become green farmland.
Dams could give water for irrigation and drinking. Red Sea water could become fresh water by **desalination** (removing salt).

cards.q: Which of these is NOT a natural resource?
cards.why: Natural resources are formed naturally. A shoe is made by people.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Technology = knowledge, skills, tools and machines.
Simple technology (Bushmen) = little change. Advanced technology (Arizona) = big change.
Desalination = removing salt from sea water.

lessons.title: Adaptation of People to the Environment

cards.title: Different places, different work
body: Eritrea has physical diversity. So weather, soil, vegetation and economic activities are different from place to place.
- fishing and salt mining on the coast
- grazing animals in dry areas
- crop farming in wet areas
**Human adaptation** is a response to the physical environment.

cards.title: Six environments
body: Tap the dots to see each environment.

cards.title: The coastal land
body: It goes from the coastline to about **5 km** inland.
The climate is arid: less than **250 mm** of rain per year. The soil is salty, so growing crops is difficult.
People adapt by **fishing**, **salt mining**, **trading** and grazing animals.
Large settlements are near the coast. Away from the coast, settlements are small and scattered.

cards.title: Changes on the coast
body: - pollution: house and factory waste goes into the sea (e.g. the cement factory in Massawa)
- fewer dugongs and turtles because of hunting
- huts of wood and grass (air moves freely); trees are cut for animal feed, firewood and utensils: deforestation
- coastal villages such as Thio, Eddi and Angel are growing into towns (urbanization)

cards.title: Eastern Lowlands
body: Places: Bada, Rahaita, Thio, Afambo (south); Mai Atal, Ghahtelai, Wadi Labka (centre); Naro, Karora, Marsa Teklai (north).
Rain: **100 to 300 mm** per year. Vegetation: grassland.
Most of it is arid. Crops grow only along river courses.

cards.title: How people adapt in the Eastern Lowlands
body: - A few people grow crops around river courses, water holes (wells and springs) and river mouths. They also divert floods from rivers to grow crops.
- Most people far from water graze animals. They move to find water and pasture.
- They live in mobile tents called **agnet**. Air moves freely in them.
- They cut trees for animal feed, firewood and fences: deforestation.

cards.title: Rainfall in each environment
body: Move the slider. Compare the rain.

states.label: Coast
states.text: Coastal land: less than 250 mm. Fishing, salt mining, trade.

states.label: East
states.text: Eastern Lowlands: 100 to 300 mm. Mostly grazing animals.

states.label: SW
states.text: South of the Western Lowlands: 600 to 800 mm. Crops and animals, using rain.

states.label: NW
states.text: North of the Western Lowlands: 200 to 300 mm. Grazing; now horticulture with irrigation.

states.label: High
states.text: Highlands: 400 to 800 mm, cool. Crop farming.

states.label: North high
states.text: Northern highlands: rugged, dry, soil not fertile. Grazing animals.

cards.title: Southern Western Lowlands
body: They include most of Gash-Barka Region and the lowlands of Anseba Region.
The south is wetter (600 to 800 mm). Farmers grow crops and keep animals using rainfall.
There were dense woodlands, e.g. around Shilalo and Shambko. People cleared and burned them to get farmland.

cards.title: Crops of the southern Western Lowlands
head: Type
Crops
rows: orange, tangerine, lemon, grape (Shambiko); bananas (Haikota, Binbina)

cards.title: Northern Western Lowlands
body: Akurdet, Sawa and Hagaz are dry: **200 to 300 mm** per year.
Before independence, most land was used for grazing. People kept many animals because wealth depended on the number of animals.
This led to **over-grazing** and deforestation.

cards.title: Horticulture today
body: Today **horticulture** (growing fruits and vegetables) is growing fast, using groundwater for irrigation:
- vegetables between Hagaz and Akurdet
- vegetables at Afhimbol, near Sawa
- banana, papaya, orange, tangerine and lemon at Akurdet
But horticulture, roads, villages, towns and grazing together cause deforestation.

cards.title: The highlands
body: Cool climate, **400 to 800 mm** of rain. Maekel Region, western Debub Region and Hazemo have deep, fertile soils. So people grow crops.
Towns grow fast, so more vegetables are grown with irrigation.
Farms are very small. Soil erosion is high because vegetation was removed.

cards.title: Changing the highlands
body: To conserve soil and water: steep slopes are **terraced**, trees are planted, dams and ponds are built.
Many roads are built. Villages and towns grow.
The **northern highlands** are rugged, dry and not fertile. People graze animals. The land is over-grazed; branches are cut for animal feed.

cards.q: The mobile tent used in the Eastern Lowlands is called:
cards.why: The textbook says they live in mobile tents (agnet) that allow free air circulation.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Coast: fishing. Eastern Lowlands: grazing. SW lowlands: crops + animals.
NW lowlands: grazing, now horticulture. Highlands: crops. Northern highlands: grazing.
Everywhere people change the environment (deforestation, roads, towns).

cards.title: Why are trees cut?
body: Most rural people live by growing crops and grazing animals. Cash crops (coffee, cotton, citrus fruits, sesame) also come from land.
So vegetation was cut to get:
- land for crops, vegetables and fruits
- animal feed, firewood and charcoal
- building materials (houses, utensils, ploughs, chairs, tables)
This is **deforestation**.

steps.text: 1. **High erosion**: bare soil is washed away.
2. **Shortage of fuel wood**. People burn crop remains, herbs and animal dung. The soil loses nutrients, so crops become poor.
3. **Shortage of timber** for building houses.
4. Wild animals lose their homes (habitats), so there are **fewer wild animals**.
5. More water is **lost by evaporation** from the soil in the dry period.
6. **Shortage of water** for drinking and irrigation.

cards.title: Decrease of soil fertility
body: Soil is the basic resource of agriculture. Good soil gives high crop yields.
Soil erosion is one of Eritrea's most serious problems. It makes soil shallow and less fertile.
Result: less crop production.

cards.title: Memory trick: why soil becomes poor

letters.m: Absence of fallowing and crop rotation

body: **Do Over, Over Again**: farming the same way again and again makes soil poor.

cards.title: Wild animals in danger
body: Most of Eritrea is grassland, an ideal home for wildlife.
Decades ago Eritrea had many wild animals.
- elephants, hippopotamus, buffalo, giraffe, greater kudu, wild ass
- Nubian ibex, waterbuck, lion, leopard, cheetah, monkeys
- green turtles and dugongs
Today they are few. They are **endangered animals**.

cards.title: Memory trick: why animals decrease
body: Four causes: **V-D-W-H**. Say: "Very Dry Wars Hurt".

cards.title: Where wild animals live today
body: Tap the dots to see the places.

cards.title: Animals and places
head: Place
Animals

gazelle, green turtle, dugong, giant Arabian bustard

cards.title: Pollution of the sea
body: Marine resources need clean water. But the sea is polluted by:
- domestic (household) waste dumped into the sea
- port activities when ships and boats are loaded and unloaded
- industrial sewage and chemicals, e.g. from the cement factory
Marine pollution is dangerous to sea animals.

cards.q: Elephants are found today:
cards.why: The textbook lists elephant, warthog, bush buck, lion, leopard, baboon and monkey north of the Setit River.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Deforestation → erosion, fuel and timber shortage, fewer animals, water loss.
Soil becomes poor: deforestation, over-grazing, over-cultivation, no fallowing or rotation.
Sea pollution: household waste, ports, factories.

cards.title: Protect the trees
body: We cut trees to get farmland, because crops are a basic need.
But we must prevent deforestation. Ways: agro-forestry, afforestation, reforestation and avoiding over-grazing.

cards.title: Agro-forestry
body: **Agro-forestry** is a land use system where trees or bushes are grown together with crops. Examples:
- grow bushes round the fields; leave some trees standing when clearing land
- grow crops in the open spaces between widely spaced trees
- graze livestock where trees and grass mix, cutting only some branches for feed

cards.title: Why agro-forestry is good
body: Tap each dot to see one advantage.

cards.title: Five advantages
body: 1. Trees add nutrients to the soil (nitrogen fixation). Fallen leaves become **humus**.
2. Tree roots hold the soil and stop erosion.
3. Trees give shade for animals and for village meetings.
4. Many trees bear fruits.
5. Trees are homes for birds and climbing animals.

cards.title: Afforestation or reforestation?
head: Word
Meaning
rows: planting trees on land that was **not** a forest before
planting trees on land that **was** deforested

cards.title: Reforestation in Eritrea
body: Every summer, high school students in Eritrea plant trees and terrace slopes. They fight desertification.
The trees planted should be:
- fast growing
- drought-resistant
- termite-resistant

cards.title: Memory trick: which trees?
body: **Farmers Don't Tire**: plant trees that are Fast, resist Drought and resist Termites.

cards.title: Avoid over-grazing
body: **Over-grazing** is when there are more animals than the grass can feed.
The vegetation is uprooted and destroyed. It has little chance to grow again.
The soil becomes loose. Running water and wind easily erode it.

cards.title: Protect soil fertility
body: Roots hold the soil. Leaves and branches reduce the force of heavy rain. So:
- plant trees and use agro-forestry
- crop rotation and fallowing
- fertilizers
- terracing
- check dams, and bushes and grass along gullies

cards.title: Protect the sea and water
body: People who pollute the sea must be taught how to protect marine water.
Water shortage can be solved by:
- planting trees, bushes and grass, and terracing slopes, so water seeps down to form groundwater
- dams and ponds along water courses
- cisterns, or barrels to collect roof water in the rainy season
- using water wisely

cards.q: Planting trees in a deforested area is called:
cards.why: Reforestation = planting trees on deforested areas. Afforestation = planting where there was no forest before.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Re-forestation = forest again (it was there before).
Agro-forestry = trees + crops together.
Trees to plant: fast growing, drought-resistant, termite-resistant.

tips.text: For each environment learn **three things**: rainfall, main activity, one change. Example: Eastern Lowlands = 100–300 mm, grazing, deforestation.
Afforestation vs reforestation is a common trap. **Re** = again, so reforestation = the forest was there before.
Cause-and-effect questions: cause = deforestation, over-grazing, over-cultivation; effect = erosion, poor soil, fewer animals, less water.
Place + product pairs are easy marks: Alighidir = cotton; Shambiko = citrus; Haikota/Binbina = bananas; Afhimbol = vegetables; Massawa = cement factory.

units.title: Eritrea and Its Strategic Location
units.intro: This unit is about where Eritrea is, its size and shape, and why its place on the Red Sea is so important (strategic).

pins.text: Ras Kassar (north end of the coast)
Eritrea, in the Horn of Africa

cards.title: Where is Eritrea?
body: Eritrea is in the **Horn of Africa**, on the western shore of the **Red Sea**.
It is between **12°N and 18°N** latitude, and between **36°E and 43°E** longitude.

cards.title: Neighbours
body: Tap the dots to see the neighbours. The dashed lines are 12°N, 18°N, 36°E and 43°E.

cards.title: The coast
body: The coast of Eritrea goes from the **Djibouti border** in the south-east to **Ras Kassar** in the north.
It is about **1216 km** long.

cards.title: Memory trick: the numbers
body: The coast **1216** km starts with **12**, like the latitude 12°N. Latitude is small (12–18); longitude is bigger (36–43).

cards.q: Eritrea is bordered by the Sudan on the:
cards.why: The Sudan is on the north and west. Ethiopia is south, Djibouti south-east, the Red Sea and Yemen east.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: East: Red Sea and Yemen. South-east: Djibouti. North and west: Sudan. South: Ethiopia.
Coast: about 1216 km, Djibouti border to Ras Kassar.

cards.title: Not a small country
body: Many people think Eritrea is small. It is not!
Eritrea ranks **96th** in size out of **193** countries.
Its land area is about **124,330 km²**.

cards.title: Triangle shape
body: Eritrea is almost **triangular** in shape. It becomes much narrower towards the south-east (Djibouti).

cards.title: Six administrative regions
body: Move the slider from the smallest to the largest region.

states.label: Central
states.text: Central Region: 1,400 km². Capital: Asmara. The smallest.

states.label: Southern

states.label: S. Red Sea
states.text: Southern Red Sea Region: 23,384 km². Capital: Assab. Larger than Israel.

states.label: N. Red Sea
states.text: Northern Red Sea Region: 33,178 km². Capital: Massawa.

states.label: Gash-Barka
states.text: Gash-Barka Region: 34,539 km². Capital: Barentu. The largest.

cards.title: Regions bigger than countries
body: Gash-Barka and Northern Red Sea regions are much larger than Lesotho, Armenia, Albania, Burundi, Rwanda and Israel.
Anseba and Southern Red Sea regions are larger than Israel.

cards.title: Memory trick: region capitals
body: Small to big: **C-S-A-S-N-G**. Say: "**C**ats **S**leep **A**nd **S**nore, **N**ot **G**rowl."

cards.title: Over 360 islands
body: Eritrea has over **360 islands**. Some are larger than whole countries.
**Dahlak Kebir** (642.95 km²) is the largest. It is larger than Bahrain, Seychelles, Andorra and Malta.
Norah island is also larger than many countries.

cards.q: Which of these countries is larger than the others?
cards.why: Eritrea is 124,330 km². Bulgaria is 110,000, Holland 41,526 and Belgium 32,545 km².

cards.title: Remember this!
body: 124,330 km², 96th of 193 countries, triangular shape.
Largest region: Gash-Barka. Smallest: Central.
Largest island: Dahlak Kebir.

cards.title: An old trade route
body: Eritrea is on the western shore of the Red Sea.
For centuries the Red Sea was an important **trade route** between Africa and Asia.
Ancient Greek and Roman sources (2000 years ago) say traders came from as far as India and China.

cards.title: An ancient civilization
body: So Eritrea was part of an ancient civilization.
Recent archaeological evidence shows developed societies in Eritrea **before the Axumite period**.

steps.text: Because of its strategic location, many colonial and expansionist forces wanted Eritrea.
**1557**: the **Turks** occupied Massawa. They controlled the coast for about 300 years. Then the **Egyptians** controlled the coast and the Western Lowlands.
From the end of the 18th century the **Abyssinians** tried to put their influence on the highlands.
**1869**: the **Italians** got a foothold in **Assab**.
**1885**: the Italians occupied **Massawa**.
**1890**: for the first time, all parts of Eritrea were united under one administration (Italian).
**1941**: Italian rule collapsed. The **British** defeated Italy and ruled until 1952.
**1952**: Eritrea was forcefully **federated** with Ethiopia by a UN resolution.
**May 24, 1991**: after 30 years of struggle, Eritrea achieved **independence**. This is why we celebrate May 24.

cards.title: Federation and annexation
body: Western powers, especially Britain and the USA, supported Ethiopia for their own strategic interests.
Ethiopia dissolved the federation and made Eritrea one of its provinces. The UN did nothing.
Ethiopia's main motive: to have **access to the Red Sea**.

steps.text: The Red Sea is a long, narrow sea. It joins the **Mediterranean Sea** and the **Indian Ocean**.
A ship from Europe enters through the **Suez Canal**. It is the gateway to the Mediterranean in the north-west.
It sails down the **Red Sea**, the shortest way between Asia and Europe.
It passes the Eritrean coast: about 1216 km along this route.
It leaves through **Bab el Mandeb**, the gateway to the Indian Ocean in the south-east.

cards.title: Why the location is strategic
body: - Eritrea has a very long coast on an international sea route between Bab el Mandeb and the Suez Canal.
- The Red Sea is one of the world's **busiest waterways**. Most trade between Europe and Asia passes through it.
- Eritrea has access to the **Middle East**, which produces about **67%** of the world's petroleum and has the largest reserves.

cards.title: A rich sea
body: The Red Sea is one of the saltiest seas in the world. It is rich in marine resources.
Eritrea has full sovereignty over its territorial sea.
It has full rights over fisheries and all natural resources in it.

cards.q: Which is the gateway between the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean?
cards.why: Bab el Mandeb is the gateway to the Indian Ocean in the south-east. The Suez Canal leads to the Mediterranean.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Strategic location = on the busy Red Sea route between Europe and Asia.
Suez Canal (north-west) and Bab el Mandeb (south-east) are the two gates.
The motive of all colonial powers was to control the trade along the Red Sea route.

units.title: Colonial Expansion and Eritrean Resistance
units.intro: From the 16th to the 19th centuries, foreign powers tried to take Eritrea: the Turks, Abyssinians, Egyptians and Italians. Eritreans resisted. This unit also covers the political struggle against Ethiopian colonialism.

turks.title: Turkish possessions in the Red Sea

un.title: Proposals of the UN Inquiry Commission

tl3.title: Timeline: British period to the ELM

cards.title: The first invaders: the Turks
body: The **Turks** were the first to conduct expansion in Eritrea.
Turkish expansion in the Red Sea started in the **16th century**.
By the middle of the 16th century, the Turks controlled almost all countries in the Red Sea region.

cards.title: Turkish lands around the Red Sea
body: The red parts were Turkish. Tap the dots to see the names.

cards.title: 1557: Massawa
body: In **1557** the Turks occupied **Massawa**.
They placed their army at **Hirghigo**.
The Turkish forces were led by **Ozdemir Pasha**.

cards.title: Two conflicts
body: The Turks planned to expand to the highlands of Eritrea. This brought them into conflict with the **Bahri Negassi**.
The Turks also wanted the trade with the East and control of the Horn. So they came into conflict with the **Portuguese**.
The Portuguese also wanted to control the trade with the East (India).

cards.title: Bahri Negassi Yeshaq
body: The Bahri Negassi was the ruler of the highlands, also called **Midri Bahri**.
The capital of the Bahri Negassi was **Debarwa**.
At this time the Bahri Negassi was **Yeshaq**. He did not want the Turks to take his land. At first he stopped them.

steps.text: **1557**: The Turks occupy Massawa.
**1561**: Minas, the king of Abyssinia, wanted to attack Yeshaq. So Yeshaq made an **alliance** with the Turks and let them into the highlands. The Turks fortified Debarwa and stayed until 1567.
**1578**: Yeshaq feared an attack by the Abyssinian king **Sertse-dingle**. He invited the Turks back. Together they fought the Abyssinian king. Yeshaq was defeated and **killed**.

cards.title: After Yeshaq
body: After Yeshaq died, the highland rulers continued to resist the invaders.
Turkish rule became limited to Massawa and the coast. This rule was **nominal** (in name only).
Real power was with local rulers, the **Naibs**. They were Turkish **deputies**.

cards.q: Why did Yeshaq make an alliance with the Turks?

options.B: He feared an attack by the Abyssinian king

cards.why: Yeshaq knew it would be hard to defend against the army of Minas, the king of Abyssinia. So he allied with the Turks.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Turks = first invaders. 1557 Massawa, army at Hirghigo, leader Ozdemir Pasha.
Bahri Negassi Yeshaq, capital Debarwa, killed in 1578.
Naibs = local rulers, Turkish deputies in Massawa.

cards.title: Egypt comes through the Sudan
body: **Mohammed Ali** was the ruler of Egypt from 1805 to 1849.
He invaded the **Sudan** in **1820**. The Funj Empire at Sennar could not stop him.
By **1840** the Egyptians made their base at **Kassala**.

cards.title: Egyptian expansion, step by step
body: Move the slider. Watch Egypt move into Eritrea.

states.label: 1840s
states.text: From **Kassala** the Egyptians invaded the **Barka Valley** and the **Kunama** areas. The **Beni Amir** fell under Egyptian rule.
The **Bilen** areas were invaded. The Bet Asghede, Mensa, Maria and the upper class of the Bilen accepted Islam.
In 1846 the Turks let Mohammed Ali control Massawa for a limited time. In **1865** the Egyptians seized the **northern coast**. The Naib came under Egyptian control.
The Egyptians extended their rule to the coasts of **Dankalia**.
**Munzinger** invaded the Bogos with an Egyptian army and occupied **Keren**.
The Egyptians moved into the highlands. They were defeated at **Gundet (1875)** and **Gura (1876)**.

cards.title: Islam spreads
body: Because of Turkish and Egyptian activities, **Islam** spread to the western and eastern edges of Eritrea.

cards.title: Who was Munzinger?
body: Munzinger was a **Swiss** scholar. He lived in Massawa from 1854.
Earlier he was a consular agent for the French.
In **1871** the Egyptians made him governor of Massawa. In **1872** he occupied Keren.

cards.title: Why little resistance in the west?
body: The people were **tired of repeated invasions by the Abyssinians**. So they did not strongly oppose the Egyptians.
The local people could not stop the expansion alone.
The Europeans were afraid of Egyptian expansion. Finally they stopped the raids on the Bilen areas.

cards.title: Into the highlands: Gundet and Gura
body: **Khedive Ismail** ruled Egypt after Mohammed Ali. He wanted all of Eritrea and parts of East Africa.
He sent a large army led by a **Danish mercenary, Arendrup**.
**1875, Battle of Gundet**: the Abyssinian army of Emperor Yohannes defeated the Egyptians.
**Woldemichael Solomon** played a big role. He followed the Egyptians and captured **700 rifles**.
**1876, Battle of Gura**: the Egyptians were defeated again. They left the highlands but stayed in Bogos and on the coast.

cards.title: Memory trick: G before G
body: Gun-det is a longer word and comes first (1875). Gu-ra comes one year later (1876).

cards.title: Egypt grows weak: the Mahdist Revolt
body: In **1882** a strong movement arose in the Sudan: the **Mahdist Revolt**.
The **Mahdi** (Muhammad Ahmad) was a religious leader. He led the fight to free the Sudan from foreign control.
Under the Mahdi and his successor, the **Khalifa** (Abdallahi), the Sudan defeated the Egyptians. Khalifa means successor in Arabic.

steps.text: **1820**: Mohammed Ali of Egypt invades the Sudan.
**1840**: the Egyptians have their base at Kassala. They raid the Barka Valley and the Kunama areas.
**1853**: the Bilen areas are invaded.
**1865**: Egypt seizes the northern coast. The Naib comes under Egyptian control.
**1872**: Munzinger occupies Keren.
**1875**: the Egyptians are defeated at Gundet.
**1876**: defeated again at Gura. They leave the highlands.

cards.q: Who captured 700 rifles from the retreating Egyptians?
cards.why: After the Battle of Gundet, Woldemichael Solomon followed the retreating Egyptians and captured 700 rifles.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: 1820 Sudan, 1840 Kassala, 1853 Bilen, 1865 north coast, 1872 Keren (Munzinger).
Egypt lost at Gundet (1875) and Gura (1876).
The Mahdist Revolt (1882) weakened Egypt.

cards.title: Tribute and plunder
body: Highland Eritrea was **not part of Abyssinia**. But its rulers were forced to pay taxes (**tribute**).
Abyssinian kings and princes crossed to Medri Bahri to collect tribute or take any wealth.
In these attacks many people were **massacred** and much property was taken.

cards.title: Rivalry helps the invaders
body: In the 17th century political power moved from **Debarwa to Hazzega**.
Then the ruling houses of **Hazzega** and **Tseazzega** became rivals.
This rivalry let Abyssinian, especially Tigrean, rulers interfere.
In **1770** the Tigrean ruler **Ras Michael Sehul** deposed Bahri Negassi **Bokru** of Tseazzega. He put a man from Hazzega in his place.

cards.title: Why did Tigrean rulers want Eritrea?
body: In the 19th century Tigrean rulers fought Abyssinian kings for power.
Control of Eritrea let them: **1.** plunder Eritrea's resources; **2.** get arms through the coast.

cards.title: Playing one chief against another
body: The highland leaders did not want to lose their **sovereignty**.
So they often allied with one Abyssinian chief against another.
**Degiat Hailu** of Tseazzega fought off Agew Negusse. He also tried to ally with Tewodros against Emperor Yohannes.

cards.title: Resistance in the lowlands
body: Attacks also hit the Beni Amir, Kunama, Nara, Bogos and Semhar.
In the **Upper Barka**, **Zemat Wed Ikud** protected the people from Tigrean plunderers.
The tribes formed **alliances**: with the Mahdists against the Abyssinians, and sometimes they asked the Egyptians for protection.

cards.title: The Saho, Mensa and Bilen
body: The **Saho** cooperated with **Bahta Hagos** against the forces of Yohannes.
They fought successfully against **Ras Araya at Ruba Haddas** and against **Ras Alula at Rub-Rubia**.
Continuous Tigrean and Amhara invasions finally forced the Saho to submit to the Italians. Soon Saho patriots fought the Italians too.
The **Mensa and Bilen** cooperated with Woldemichael against the forces of Yohannes.

cards.title: Ras Woldemichael Solomon
body: Ras Woldemichael was based in **Hazzega**. He strongly opposed foreign expansion.
Sometimes he used the expansionists to make his position stronger.
He defeated **Deggiat Hailu** of Tseazzega, who had Abyssinian support, at the **Battle of Wokki Duba**.
In the end **Ras Alula** captured him and sent him into **exile** in Tigray.

cards.q: What helped the Abyssinians to interfere in the Eritrean highlands?
cards.why: The rivalry between the ruling houses of Hazzega and Tseazzega gave Tigrean and Abyssinian rulers the chance to interfere.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Disunity (Hazzega against Tseazzega) opened the door to invaders.
1770: Ras Michael Sehul deposed Bahri Negassi Bokru.
Woldemichael won at Wokki Duba but was exiled by Ras Alula.

cards.title: Europeans in the Red Sea
body: The **Suez Canal** opened in **1869**. It made the Red Sea more important.
The British occupied **Aden** in 1839 and took control of Egypt in 1882. The French got the port of **Djibouti**.
Italian missionaries were active in Eritrea: **Giuseppe Sapeto**, **Giustino de Jacobis** and **Giovanni Stella**.

cards.title: Buying Assab
body: In **1869** Giuseppe Sapeto bought the village of **Assab** from Sultan Ibrahim. He bought it for the **Rubattino Shipping Company**.
In **1882** the Italian government bought all the coastal land and set up an administration in Assab.

cards.title: Why did Britain help Italy?
body: The Italians knew the Mahdists had weakened Egypt. They feared the Abyssinians might take Egyptian land.
The **British** did not want their rival, **France**, to control more of the coast. So they **encouraged the Italians** to occupy these areas.

cards.title: Italian expansion, step by step
body: Move the slider. Watch Italy spread from the coast.

states.text: **Assab**: bought by Sapeto in 1869; Italian government administration in 1882.
On **February 5, 1885** the Italians took over **Massawa**.
In 1886 they moved to Seatit and Wia. In **January 1887** Ras Alula defeated them at **Dogali**. In 1888 they took Seatit again.
**Keren** in July 1889, **Asmara** in August 1889. Then they reached the **Mereb and Belesa** rivers.
On **January 1, 1890** King Umberto I of Italy named the new colony **Eritrea**.

cards.title: Why could Italy expand?
body: **1.** The local people were tired of Abyssinian attacks, especially by Tigrean warlords.
**2.** The **Great Famine** weakened the people's ability to resist.
**3.** The British encouraged the Italians. The Italians also used force against resistance.
In 1889 Emperor Yohannes died fighting the Mahdists. Ras Alula took his forces back to Tigray. This opened the way for Italy.

cards.title: Treaties and borders
body: **May 2, 1889: Treaty of Wuchale** with Minilik of Abyssinia. It recognized Italian possession of most of eastern Eritrea.
**Additional Convention (October 1889)**: all lands occupied by Italy were put inside its boundary.
**Treaty of Addis Ababa (1896)**: Ethiopia again recognized Italian possessions.
Boundary delimitations were made in 1900, 1902 and 1908.

cards.q: Who named the colony Eritrea, and when?
cards.why: On January 1, 1890 King Umberto I of Italy named his new colony Eritrea.

cards.title: From friends to enemies
body: At first many Eritrean leaders supported the Italians. They were tired of Abyssinian attacks.
Then the Italians followed **harsh policies**: **a.** they took land from the people and gave it to Italians; **b.** Eritrean leaders were arrested.
So many Eritrean leaders turned against them.

cards.title: Where the patriots fought
body: Tap the dots. X = a battle.

cards.title: Zemat Wed Ikud
body: Zemat Wed Ikud was a **Beni Amir** from the village of Ali Bekit. He controlled the **Upper Barka**.
He resisted Italian expansion strongly. The Italians sent a relative who tricked him out of hiding.
He was imprisoned in **Nakura** and died there.

cards.title: Nakura prison
body: Nakura is one of the **Dahlak Islands**.
The Italians chose it for a prison because it is **remote and isolated**. It is also very hot.

cards.title: Ali Mohammed Usman Burri
body: He was an **Afar**, imprisoned in Nakura for opposing the Italians.
On **November 17, 1899** he and some prisoners set free **102 prisoners** and escaped by boat. The boat landed at **Burri**.
Degiat Mahray and Blatta Gerezgiher Gilay escaped with him.
He is honoured as the **'jail-breaker of Nakura'**.

cards.title: Degiat Aberra Hailu
body: Born in **1840** in **Tseazzega**. His father had the title 'Cantiba'.
The Italians sent 100 soldiers under **Captain Bettini** to capture him.
Aberra defeated them and Bettini was killed: the **Battle of Walta Medhanit (March 1892)**, near Dekki Shehai in Anseba.
He fled to Tigray. After 1896 (Adwa) he had to leave Tigray. He moved to Shewa and died there.

cards.title: Degiat Bahta Hagos
body: In **1875** he refused to pay tribute to the Tigrean chief **Fitawrari Embaye**. Embaye was killed. Bahta fled to the Habab area in the Sahil.
Later he welcomed the Italians and got arms from them. In 1889 they made him governor of **Akkele Guzai** (title Degiat) for five years.
He turned against them because they took land from peasants (**land expropriation**).
In **1894** he revolted and imprisoned Lieutenant **Sanguinetti**. He was killed at the **Battle of Halay, December 1894**.

cards.title: Abubaker Ahmed
body: He led **Saho and Tigrigna** fighters.
In **1901** he fought 200 Italian soldiers with only **20 men**. The battle lasted five hours.
Italians: 2 killed, 4 wounded. His side: 1 killed, 4 wounded.
The Italians tried many times to capture him but failed. He was finally killed in battle.

cards.title: Mohammed Nuri
body: Mohammed Nuri was a **Saho**. He escaped from Nakura and attacked the Italians from Tigray.
In **1902** he was at Adi Rosso. People believed he planned to kill **Martini**, the Italian governor.

cards.title: Mahber Fiqri Hager (1941)
body: In **1941** the British replaced the Italians. The British were against Eritrean independence.
In 1941 **Mahber Fiqri Hager** was formed. It was an **anti-colonial** association. It also protected the social and economic needs of Eritreans.
Founders included **Ghebremesqel Woldu**, **Woldeab Woldemariam** and **Ibrahim Sultan**.
It opposed colonialism and demanded an end to Italian privileges. It laid the foundation for political parties.

The Unionist Party was formed with Ethiopian support. The Pro-Italy Party had Italian and Eritrean members.

So the issue went to the **UN**. The UN also could not agree.
A **UN Inquiry Commission** came to Eritrea from **February 4 to April 6, 1950** to find out what Eritreans wanted.

body: On **December 2, 1950**, by **Resolution 390A (V)**, the UN General Assembly joined Eritrea with Ethiopia in a **Federation**.

It weakened Eritrea's economy. It shut down trade unions and political parties. The press was not free.

body: The **Eritrean Liberation Movement (ELM)** was set up in **Port Sudan** in **1958**.
Its members were Moslems and Christians, lowlanders and highlanders.
It was made of cells of **seven** members, so it was called **Mahber Showatte**. In the lowlands it was called **Harakat**.
Its aim: build an organization in the government and police to bring about a **coup**.

cards.title: The end of the ELM
body: Later the ELM tried armed struggle. By then the **ELF** had appeared.
In **1965** the ELF defeated a small ELM force at **Illa Tsada**.
This and Ethiopian suppression led to the decline of the ELM.

units.title: Colonial Administrations in Eritrea
units.intro: This unit is about the Italian and British colonial administrations in Eritrea: their structure, aims, policies and effects.

aims.title: The changing aims of Italian colonialism

pins.text: Sudan: the Italian advance was stopped
Massawa: port improved, naval base; the floating dock was later sold to Pakistan
Western Eritrea: the British wanted to join it to the Sudan

cards.title: Why colonies?
body: Between 1869 and 1890 Italy expanded in Eritrea. By 1890 all of Eritrea was an **Italian colony**.
Colonialists use the **wealth** of the colonies for their own benefit.
They do this with **colonial policies**. The policies are applied through a colonial **administration**.

steps.text: **At the beginning**: to let **Italian farmers settle** in Eritrea.
**Later**: to make it possible to **export Italian goods** to Eritrea.
**In the end**: to build facilities to make the **Italian conquest of Ethiopia** possible.

cards.title: What is administration for?
body: The purpose of administration is to **put government policy into practice**.
So the Italians set up their own administration.

cards.title: Direct control
body: In both the highlands and the lowlands the Italians made sure they had **direct control** of the people.

cards.title: The highlands: mislene
body: Districts had existed in the highlands for a long time. The Italians kept some, changed some and made new ones.
They appointed traditional leaders, closely controlled by Italian administrators (**commissari**).
These appointed leaders were called **mislene**. They were paid salaries.
They lost their power but kept privileges: the right to **collect taxes** and to **work as judges**.

cards.title: The lowlands: tribal groups
body: In the lowlands the administration was based on traditional **tribal and geographical** groups.
Traditional leaders kept their positions and payments from **serfs**. But they lost their power.
The serf now had to recognize **only the Italian administration**. The leaders no longer had to protect the serf.
In **1934** the Italians began paying salaries to some important leaders. This stopped in 1941.

cards.title: Municipalities
body: In the towns the Italians set up **municipalities** (town governments).
The **seven** principal towns had municipalities: **Asmara, Massawa, Keren, Dekemhare, Adi Ugri, Adi Keih and Assab**.

Appeals went to **higher courts** with **Italian judges**.
Appointed judges got money from **salaries** and **fines** on wrongdoers.

cards.title: Notables and employees
body: **Notabile** (notables) were not paid salaries. They got economic benefits instead.
Notables included religious leaders of Islamic communities and heads of monasteries.
Later a few Eritreans worked for the Italian government as **interpreters, telegraphists and clerks**.

cards.title: The Racial Laws (1937)
body: The Italians believed colonizers were **superior** to the colonized.
The **Racial Laws** were introduced formally in **1937**. They separated colonizers from the colonized at all levels.
Italians were forbidden to interact with or marry Eritrean women.
Eritreans could not move freely outside 'native areas'. For example, they could not use the main street in Asmara (**Liberation Avenue**).
Eritreans could not use public services such as bars used by Italians.

cards.title: Education only to grade 4
body: Eritreans were **not allowed to learn beyond grade 4**.
The aim was not experts. It was people with **low skills** and people who would be **obedient subjects**.

cards.q: Up to which grade could Eritreans learn under the Italians?
cards.why: The Racial policies in education did not allow Eritreans to learn beyond grade 4.

cards.title: Industrialization
body: Industrialization means building plants and facilities (factories, mines, roads) to **exploit** Eritrea.
It happened because of: **a.** military needs; **b.** needs of Italian settlers; **c.** agriculture and mining.
The Italians expanded Asmara, Massawa, Adi Ugri, Dekemhare and Keren, and built roads to link them.
To prepare the invasion of Ethiopia they built **ports, airports, power stations**, and telephone and telegraph systems.

cards.title: The Second World War
body: The Second World War was fought from **1939 to 1945**.
**Axis Powers**: Italy, Japan and Germany. **Allied Powers**: the USA, Britain, France and the USSR.
The British fought Italy in North and North-east Africa.

steps.text: Allied attacks under the British **stopped the Italian advance in the Sudan**.
The Italians **retreated** from **Tessenei** and **Agordat**.
The Italians resisted at **Keren**, but in **March 1941** they were defeated.
In **April 1941** the British occupied **Asmara**. Soon they set up the **British Military Administration (BMA)**.

cards.title: Temporary rule and the Hague Convention
body: Unlike Italy, British occupation was meant to be **temporary**.
The **Hague Convention (1907)** said how it should work. It required the British to rule **humanely** and in the interest of Eritreans.
But the British only cared about **their own interests**.

cards.title: What did the British do?
body: Move the slider. Tap the dots too.

states.label: War base
states.text: Eritrea was a base for supplying British forces in the Middle East. They **improved the port of Massawa** and built a **naval base** there. They built an **ammunition store in Ghinda**. In **Asmara** they built facilities to repair civilian aircraft.

states.label: Weaken
states.text: To weaken Eritrea economically they **destroyed factories and machinery**. They **sold the floating dock at Massawa to Pakistan**. They **removed the railroad up to Akurdet**.

states.label: Divide
states.text: They wanted to join **Western Eritrea** to the **Sudan**, a British colony. So they encouraged **ethnic division**.

cards.title: Broken promises
body: The British did not keep their promise of **self-government**. All political activities were forbidden.
They supported the Italians. They employed Italians in the administration and the courts. Their laws protected Italian land and property.
Only Italians could open factories and start businesses.
Long-term aim: keep Eritrea **economically weak and disunited**.

cards.title: Administration
body: The British kept the Italian administrative organization.
They did not have enough staff, so the divisions were reduced to **five**.

cards.q: Why did the British want Eritrea to stay weak and divided?

options.A: To join Western Eritrea to the Sudan

cards.why: The British hoped to control Western Eritrea and join it to the Sudan, which was a British colony.

cards.title: Reforms
body: The **Eritrean police force** was filled by Eritreans from the start, under British command. It replaced the Carabinieri and the Polizia Africana Italiana.
Some Eritreans got higher jobs, such as police inspectors and Administration Assistants.
The **Racial Law** was more and more ignored and finally **abolished**.
**Native Courts** were opened and replaced the Italian Residenti courts.
Education improved: Eritreans could study **beyond Grade 4**. The British tried to give Eritreans better health facilities than the Italians did.

cards.title: The economy after the war
body: During the war, Middle East markets helped industry for manufactured goods in Eritrea.
After the war these goods could not compete with goods from Europe.
So attention moved to **agriculture and livestock**. Efforts were made to be self-sufficient in vegetables, fruit and grain.

cards.title: The result
body: The reforms were limited and had little effect. British policies had serious long-term bad effects.
But they also **increased political awareness**. The wish for freedom and independence became strong.

The p. 103 summary adds: maintain law and order, respect rights, assist in development.
questions.tip: The British did the opposite: only their own interests.

similar.q: When was the Hague Convention?

questions.q: Give two ways the British weakened Eritrea economically.
questions.answer: They destroyed factories and machinery, sold the floating dock at Massawa to Pakistan, and removed the railroad up to Akurdet.
why: The textbook lists three: destroyed factories and machinery; sold the floating dock to Pakistan; removed the railroad up to Akurdet.
questions.tip: Factories, dock, railroad.

similar.q: Which part of Eritrea did the British want to join to the Sudan?

questions.q: Because of too few staff, the British reduced the administrative divisions to:
why: The British kept the Italian organization but reduced the number of divisions to five.
questions.tip: Italy 8, Britain 5.
