units.title: Highlights of the Eritrean Armed Struggle
units.intro: This unit tells why the armed struggle began, how it developed (ELF and EPLF), and how it ended with liberation in 1991.

elf.title: ELF leadership: far from the fighters

pins.text: PLF-1, the Dankalia group: Sudoha-Ela, June-July 1970
PLF-2, the Ala group: from Hamasien to Akkele Guzai
Ubel group (ELF split) in the Barka region

cards.title: Why the armed struggle?
body: The Second World War ended in 1945. Then the future of the former Italian colonies (**Libya, Eritrea and Somalia**) was a question.
It went first to the Four Great Powers and then to the UN.
As a former colony, Eritrea had the right to **self-determination** and independence. It was **denied** this right.
On **December 2, 1950** the UN decided to federate Eritrea with Ethiopia, in the interest of the Western Powers.

cards.title: Federation, then violations
body: The Federation was set up on **September 11, 1952**.
Soon Ethiopia systematically **violated** the Federal Act.
In **1958** the ELM was set up against these violations. Its aims were a coup and independence. The ELM was **not** devoted to armed struggle.

cards.title: The ELF and the first shot
body: At the beginning of the 1960s, Eritrean **exiles** who opposed the ELM formed an armed organization.
The **ELF** was established in **1960**. It was dedicated to **armed struggle**.
On **September 1, 1961** **Hamid Idris Awate** fired the first shot at **Mount Adal**. The armed struggle began.

cards.title: Memory trick: 9-1-1961
body: **A**wate at **A**dal: two As. September **1**, 19**61**: the struggle begins with shot number **1**.

cards.title: A leadership far from the field
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Supreme Council
states.text: The three leaders made up the **Supreme Council**, the highest political body.

states.label: Revolutionary Council
states.text: The **Revolutionary Council** was in charge of military affairs. It was based in **Kassala**.

states.label: ELA
states.text: The **ELA** was the military wing of the ELF. It grew steadily. The leadership was **removed from the fighters** in the field.

cards.title: Divide and rule
body: The ELF leaders felt threatened by the growing ELA. To keep their positions they used **divide and rule**.
In **1964** the ELA was divided into **4** sections on **ethnic lines**: four **Zonal Commands**.
A **fifth** zone was added in **1965**.

cards.title: The Zonal Commands
body: Move the slider. The lines are only a rough copy of Figure 7.2.

states.text: **1964**: four Zonal Commands.
**1965**: a fifth zone was added.

states.label: Anseba 1968
states.text: **Anseba Conference (September 18, 1968)**: zones 1 and 2 did not come. Zones **3, 4 and 5** formed the **Joint Force** (Provisional Revolutionary Command).

states.label: Adobha 1969
states.text: **Adobha Conference (1969)**: all Zonal Commands came. Zones 1 and 2 accepted the Joint Force. A new leadership appeared: **Kiad Al Amma** (General Command).

cards.title: Problems grow
body: The ELF grew and won some victories.
But its poor policies and methods caused many civilian deaths and fighters' **casualties**.
Many fighters were unhappy. **Defections** took place, especially in **1967**. Clearly the ELF had to change.

steps.text: **1964–1965**: Zonal Commands divide the fighters.
**1967**: many fighters defect.
**1968, Aredaib Meeting**: remove the Zonal Command structure; set up a **field-based leadership**. **Anseba Conference** (September 18): the **Joint Force**.
**1969, Adobha Conference**: **Kiad Al Amma** (General Command). It planned a national conference on reform.

cards.title: Reform fails
body: Kiad Al Amma soon **violated** the Adobha provisions.
It became clear the ELF could not be reformed from within.
Many fighters left and formed **splinter groups**. Ethnic or regional motives also caused division.

cards.q: Which Zonal Commands formed the Joint Force at the Anseba Conference?
cards.why: The First and Second Zonal Commands did not attend. The Third, Fourth and Fifth formed the Joint Force.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: 1960 ELF; September 1, 1961 first shot (Awate, Mount Adal).
1964 four zones, 1965 five zones (divide and rule).
1968 Aredaib and Anseba (Joint Force); 1969 Adobha (Kiad Al Amma).

cards.title: Three groups left the ELF
body: The **EPLF** came from the joining of **three factions** that left the ELF.

cards.title: The three groups
body: Move the slider. Tap the dots.

states.label: PLF-1
states.text: **Dankalia group, PLF-1**: fighters went to the Sudan, then through **Aden** to Dankalia. They formed the Eritrean People's Liberation Forces at **Sudoha-Ela** in June-July **1970**.

states.label: PLF-2
states.text: **Ala group, PLF-2**: first based in the plateau (**Hamasien**), then moved to **Akkele Guzai**.

states.label: Ubel
states.text: **Ubel** (Eritrean Liberation Forces): split from the ELF and went to **Ubel in the Barka** region.

cards.title: The EPLF is born
body: PLF-1 and PLF-2 agreed on full union in **September 1973**. They became the **EPLF**.
In **1974** the rest of the Ubel group joined the EPLF.

cards.title: Civil war (1972-1974)
body: The ELF attacked the splinter groups. A **civil war** went on from **1972 to 1974**, with some ceasefires.
Many fighters were killed. The Ubel group suffered badly from Kiad Al Amma's attacks.

cards.title: Struggle on all fronts
body: From the start the EPLF had a **clear political program**.
Its policy: conduct the **armed, political, social and economic** struggle at the same time.
Activities: **land reform, transportation, production, health care, education, relief assistance**.

cards.q: When was the NDP issued?
cards.why: The NDP was issued at the First Congress of the EPLF in 1977. It was re-affirmed in 1987.

cards.title: Working together, winning towns
body: In 1974 the civil war calmed down. In **November 1974** the EPLF and ELF agreed to coordinate military operations.
Their attacks became more and more successful.

cards.title: Towns captured by 1977
body: Green dots: towns captured by the ELF and EPLF by 1977. Tap to reveal the names. Black dots: Asmara, Massawa, Assab.

cards.title: Memory trick: the 1977 towns
body: Nine towns: **N-A-K-D-M-A-T-G-E**. Say "**Nak** **Dmat** **Ge**" three times.

cards.title: Strategic retreat (1978)
body: In **1977** the **Soviet Union** began giving massive military help to Ethiopia. **Southern Yemen** and **Cuba** also helped Ethiopia.
In **July 1978** the Soviet Union carried out a huge sea, air and land attack on Eritrean forces.
The EPLF withdrew to its base area in **Sahil**. It defended its positions, and hundreds of thousands of enemy soldiers were killed.
Slowly the EPLF began **counter-offensives**.

cards.title: The end of the ELF (1980)
body: In **1980** full-scale fighting broke out between the ELF and the EPLF.
It began after the ELF withdrew from the north-eastern Sahil front. The EPLF saw this as breaking a joint agreement.
The ELF was driven out of Eritrea into the **Sudan**. It ended as a fighting force inside Eritrea.

steps.text: **1978**: strategic retreat to the base area in **Sahil**.
**March 17–19, 1988**: the EPLF defeats the **Nadew Command** and captures **Afabet**. This is the **turning point**. Ethiopian forces withdraw from the Western Lowlands.
**February 1990, Operation Fenkil**: the coastal plains north of Massawa and **Massawa** are liberated.
**April 1990**: attack in the south. **Senafe, Adi Keih** and large parts of Akkele Guzai are liberated.
**May 1990**: **Tio, Bada, Eddi and Beilul** in the Danakil region are captured.
**May 13, 1991**: the final attack starts. **May 24, 1991**: EPLF forces enter **Asmara**.
By **May 27, 1991** the rest of Dankalia, including **Assab**, is liberated. Ethiopian colonial rule ends.

cards.q: Which battle was the turning point of the war?
cards.why: The textbook says a turning point came when the EPLF defeated the Nadew Command and captured Afabet (17–19 March 1988).

steps.text: **1977**: First Congress and the NDP; many towns captured.
**1978**: strategic retreat to Sahil.
**1980**: the ELF is driven into the Sudan.
**1987**: Second and Unity Congress re-affirms the NDP.
**1988**: victory at Afabet.
**1990**: Operation Fenkil (February), the south (April), Danakil (May).
**1991**: Asmara (May 24) and Assab (May 27). Eritrea is liberated.

body: EPLF = PLF-1 (Sudoha-Ela, 1970) + PLF-2 (Ala) in September 1973; Ubel joined in 1974.
NDP 1977; re-affirmed 1987 (pluralism, mixed economy, women's rights).
Afabet 1988 (turning point), Fenkil 1990, Asmara May 24, 1991.

units.title: Post-Independence Developments in Eritrea
units.intro: This unit covers what happened after Liberation: the Referendum and the development programs.

pins.text: Massawa: new international airport; port being modernized
Assab: end of the 600 km road from Massawa

cards.title: The first big task
body: After Liberation, the first major task of the government was to gain **recognition** from the outside world.
For this purpose a **Referendum** was held.

cards.title: Two independence days
body: **Actual** independence: **May 24, 1991**.
**Formal** independence: **May 24, 1993**, through the Referendum.

cards.title: What is a referendum?
body: A **referendum** is direct voting by citizens. It finds out whether they support or oppose something.
The people of Eritrea were asked: do you support or oppose **independence**?

cards.title: The result
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Yes
states.text: Over **99.8%** of voters supported independence.

states.label: Others
states.text: Less than 0.2% of the votes were not for independence. The thin red slice is almost invisible!

cards.title: Memory trick: 24 and 24
body: Same day, **May 24**, two years apart. 99.8% voted **yes** in between (April 23–25, 1993).

cards.q: On which date was Eritrea's independence officially declared?
cards.why: Actual independence was May 24, 1991. Independence was officially declared on May 24, 1993, after the Referendum.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Referendum: April 23–25, 1993. Result: over 99.8% for independence.
Observers: UN, OAU, Arab League, Non-Aligned Movement, many countries.

cards.title: The National Charter (February 1994)
body: The **National Charter** was issued at the **3rd Congress of the EPLF** in **February 1994**.
It gives the **objectives** of development programs and what must be considered.
At this congress the name **PFDJ** (People's Front for Democracy and Justice) replaced EPLF.

cards.title: What the Charter wants
head: Desired outcome
rows: effective participation of citizens in decision making
stability, justice, popular participation, fair distribution of wealth
depend on internal capabilities (self-reliance); promote national interests
close relations between the people and the leadership

cards.title: 1. National Service (1994)
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Training
states.text: All citizens aged **18–40** take **six months** of military training.

states.label: Work
states.text: Then they do **a year's work** in national development.

states.label: Aims
states.text: The aims: **a.** ensure the security and national independence of Eritrea; **b.** carry out national reconstruction.

cards.title: 2. Land Reform (1995)
body: The old landholding system was not good for development. Land was divided into small plots.
In **1995** a new land law was declared. **All land became the property of the state**.
**All Eritreans, men and women alike**, got the right to own land.
Citizens and non-citizens may invest on land.

cards.title: 3. Regional Restructuring (November 1995)
body: In **November 1995** a new administrative structure divided Eritrea into **6 regions**.
Purposes: **a.** strengthen national unity; **b.** balanced development of the regions; **c.** participation of the people.

cards.title: The six regions
body: Tap the dots to reveal the regions. The borders are only a rough guide.

cards.title: 4. The Constitution (1997)
body: A **constitution** is the basic law of the country. It says how the government is formed, what each part of government does, and the rights and responsibilities of citizens.
A **Constitutional Commission** was set up in **1994** to draft it.
The National Assembly (**Constituent Assembly**) ratified it on **May 23, 1997**. A Constituent Assembly can make or change a constitution.

cards.title: 5. National Defence
body: The **Eritrean Defence Forces (EDF)** came from the struggle for Liberation. They were reorganized as a modern army in **1994**.
The EDF has the **air force, navy and ground forces**. It defends the country.
The EDF also plays a big part in **development programs**.

cards.q: When was the Constitution ratified?
cards.why: The Commission was set up in 1994. The Constituent Assembly ratified the Constitution on May 23, 1997.

cards.title: Good neighbours
body: Good relations with neighbours and the world is a basic goal of the National Charter.
Eritrea worked for lasting peace in **Somalia**, which suffered from civil war.
It helped in **Sudan**: a peace agreement for Southern Sudan was signed in **2005**. Eritrea also helped an agreement in Eastern Sudan.

cards.title: Ethiopia's (Woyane) war of aggression
body: At first Eritrea had good relations with Ethiopia. This changed because of Ethiopia's unfriendly attitude.
In **1997** Ethiopian troops occupied the Eritrean village of **Adi Murug**. Expulsions and destruction continued in 1998.
Eritrea wanted a peaceful solution. But on **May 13, 1998** Ethiopia declared war.
Ethiopia carried out **three offensives**. Thousands were displaced. Bridges, clinics, schools, offices and houses were destroyed.

cards.title: The Algiers agreement (2000)
body: On **December 12, 2000** Eritrea and Ethiopia signed a peace agreement in **Algiers**. Mediators: the **US, the EU and the OAU**.
It set up a **Temporary Security Zone (TSZ)**, patrolled by UN peacekeepers.
An **International Boundary Commission** would study the border. Its decision would be **final and binding** (it could not be changed).

cards.title: Badme (April 2002)
body: In **April 2002** the Boundary Commission said **Badme** was Eritrean territory.
Ethiopia had used Badme as an excuse to start the war. The decision showed Ethiopia was the **aggressor**.
Eritrea accepted the decision immediately. Ethiopia has not accepted it.

cards.q: What did the Boundary Commission decide about Badme?

options.D: It is part of the TSZ

cards.why: In April 2002 the Boundary Commission announced that Badme was Eritrean territory.

cards.title: 6. Infrastructure
body: Move the slider. Tap the dots.

states.label: Road
states.text: Hundreds of kilometres of roads built or maintained, including the **600 km Massawa–Assab road**.

states.label: Railway
states.text: The **railway between Asmara and Massawa** has been re-activated.

states.label: Air and sea
states.text: A new **international airport** in Massawa; steps to modernize the **port of Massawa**. A national airline has started.

states.label: Power
states.text: The **Hirghigo power station** is bringing electricity to different areas.

states.label: Health
states.text: Clinics and health centres were built. Figure 8.3 shows hospitals at **Ghinda** and **Barentu**.

cards.title: More services
body: Telecommunication and postal services improved.
Radio and television were modernized and expanded.
Energy is used more efficiently, for example with the **Adhanet** (smokeless oven).

cards.title: Food self-sufficiency
body: **Self-sufficiency in food** is a major focus.
Tasks: dams and irrigation, modern farming, livestock, fishing, fighting soil erosion, re-afforestation.

cards.title: Education and health
body: The number of schools grew **fourfold**, with care for remote areas. Thousands of new teachers were trained.
The national curriculum was revised. Higher education was re-organized.
Programs fight killer diseases: **malaria, TB, HIV/AIDS** and others.

cards.title: Care for people in need
body: Care for orphans and the poor.
Help for displaced citizens, war-disabled fighters and families of the martyrs.

cards.title: Warsai-Yikaalo (May 8, 2002)
body: On **May 8, 2002** the government declared a plan for economic **recovery and reconstruction**: the **Warsai-Yikaalo** Development Campaign.
Aim: rapid progress in all sectors. Work on roads, housing, dams, fisheries, agriculture and water.
The **EDF** would be the main force. Money: internal resources and loans. Foreign companies would be invited.
Strong focus on **human resources**: new colleges and technical institutes.

steps.text: **1991** (May 24): actual independence.
**1993**: Referendum (April 23–25); independence declared May 24.
**1994**: National Charter (February); National Service; EDF reorganized; Constitutional Commission.
**1995**: new land law; six regions (November).
**1997**: Adi Murug occupied; Constitution ratified (May 23).
**1998** (May 13): Ethiopia declares war.
**2000** (December 12): peace agreement in Algiers.
**2002**: Badme decision (April); Warsai-Yikaalo (May 8).
**2005**: peace agreement for Southern Sudan.

units.title: Economic Activities in Eritrea
units.intro: People work to make a living: they grow crops, raise animals, fish, trade and work in industries. These are economic activities.

pins.text: Central and Southern highlands: taff, wheat, barley, sorghum, maize, African millet
Pearl millet: Gash-Barka, Anseba, Northern Red Sea
Eastern escarpment: coffee (Semenawi Bahri, Debubawi Bahri)
Coast south of Massawa: fishing and salt
Dahlak Archipelago: very high fish diversity
Hawakil Bay islands: high fish diversity
Lake Bordele, Buri Peninsula: sea salt
Massawa: fishing is the main activity south of here

cards.title: What are economic activities?
body: **Economic activities** are what people do to make a living.
Examples: growing crops, raising animals, working in factories, trade and fishing.

cards.title: Why so many activities?
body: Eritrea has **climatic and physical diversity**. This gives a diversity of economic activities.
Altitude goes from **120 m below sea level** (Danakil Depression) to about **3013 m** (Mount Soira).
Temperature: less than **19°C** in the highlands, more than **30°C** on the coast.
The coast and parts of the western lowlands are hot and arid.
The eastern escarpment (**Semenawi Bahri**) is temperate and sub-humid.

cards.title: Farming is the main activity
body: **Farming** is growing crops and rearing animals.
About **80%** of the people depend on crop and animal farming.
About **25%** of the land is suitable for crops, but only a small part of it is cultivated.
Most cultivated land depends on **rainfall**; the rest is irrigated.

cards.title: Different places, different work
body: **Crop production** is the main activity in the cool, wet **highlands**.
**Raising animals** is more important in the **lowlands**.
**Fishing and salt mining** are important on the coast from south of Massawa to the Djibouti border.
Examples: Irefaile, Ingel, Harena, Thio and Eddi.

cards.title: A. Traditional crop farming
body: Most people depend on **traditional farming**.
A **plough** breaks the soil. It is pulled by a pair of **oxen**; **camels** are also used in the lowlands.
Seeds are sown by hand and covered by ploughing.
Main crops: **cereals, pulses and oil seeds**.

cards.title: Contour ploughing
body: Move the slider. Compare the two ways.

states.label: Up and down
states.text: Furrows go **up and down** the slope. Rain water runs straight down and carries soil away.

states.label: Contour
states.text: **Contour ploughing**: the slope is ploughed **horizontally**. The **furrows** trap rain water and **reduce erosion**.

cards.title: Keeping the soil fertile
body: Traditional farmers use **crop rotation** and **fallowing**. These increase soil fertility.
A **furrow** is a long cut between two ridges made by a plough.
Farms are **small in the highlands** (many people) and **larger in the lowlands** (few people).

cards.title: Two seasons, double cropping
body: Some farmers farm twice: in their villages in **summer** and on the coastal plains in **autumn**.
They live in the east of Southern Region, in Central Region and in Mensae (Anseba).
Peasants on the Red Sea coast have **double cropping**. In summer they use **flood irrigation** from highland floods. They farm again in their own rainy season in autumn.
They plant water melon right after the summer harvest. The soil is fertile **alluvial** soil from highland streams.

cards.q: Where is double cropping practised in Eritrea?
cards.why: Peasants on the Red Sea coasts enjoy double cropping: floods in summer and their own rainy season in autumn.

cards.title: Crop map
body: Move the slider. Tap the dots too. Region borders are only a rough guide.

states.label: Cereals
states.text: Taff, wheat, barley, sorghum, maize and African millet grow in the highlands of **Central and Southern Regions**. Sorghum is also wide in Anseba and Gash-Barka.

states.label: Pearl millet
states.text: **Pearl millet** grows in Gash-Barka, Anseba and Northern Red Sea Regions.

states.label: Sesame
states.text: **Sesame** grows mainly in the **south-west lowlands**. People press it to make oil.

states.label: Groundnut
states.text: **Groundnuts** grow around **Keren, Adi Quala** and parts of **Gash-Barka**.

states.label: Cotton
states.text: **Cotton** grows mostly at **Alighider** in Gash-Barka. The Asmara textile industry gets its cotton from there.

states.label: Coffee
states.text: **Coffee** came from **Yemen** in the second half of the 19th century. Main areas: **Semenawi Bahri** and **Debubawi Bahri**.

states.label: Coast
states.text: The coast south of Massawa: **fishing and salt mining**.

cards.title: Uses of oil seeds and pulses
body: Oil seeds give **food oil**. Linseed is also used as a sauce and for drinking.
Linseed, Niger seed and sunflower grow in the highlands of Central and Southern Regions.
Pulses are mainly used for **sauce**. All cereals are eaten with a sauce of one of the pulses.

cards.title: Memory trick: sorting crops

letters.m: grains for bread and injera: taff, wheat, barley...
for sauce: chick pea, beans, lentil...

body: **C-O-P**: Cereals (grains), Oil seeds (oil), Pulses (sauce). Groundnut is an oil seed, not a pulse!

cards.title: B. Modern (commercial) farming
body: **Commercial farming** produces crops **for sale**.
It uses machinery, fertilizers, selected seeds, pesticides, insecticides and irrigation. So production is very high.
It was introduced by the **Italians** and developed in the British and Federation periods.

cards.title: Horticulture after independence
body: After independence commercial farming is growing fast. It focuses on **horticultural crops**: **vegetables and fruits**.
It is found near **river banks, dams and wells**, where there is water for irrigation.
Largest farms: **Alighidir Cotton Plantation, Elabered, Sawa Agro-Industries, Afhimbol**.
Main crops: banana, onion, papaya, tomato, peppers, citrus fruits, mango. Some farms grow coffee and tobacco.

cards.title: Fruits and where they grow
head: Fruit
Places
rows: Goluge, Haikota, Akurdet, Keren, Filfil, Solomuna
Ghindae, Ala, Filfil, Solomuna, Keren, Elabered, Binbina

mango, papaya, guava, peach, date palm, water melon

cards.title: Bananas and vegetables
body: Bananas are tropical fruits, rich in **carbohydrates**. They also have phosphorus, potassium and vitamins A and C.
In Eritrea fruits are grown mostly **for sale**.
Vegetables grow in all regions: onion, garlic, tomatoes, potatoes, cabbages, salad, pumpkin, carrots, cauliflower.

cards.title: Fibre crops
body: **Fibre** is a hair-like thread. It is made into yarns.
From animals: **wool** from sheep, **fur** from goats. From plants: **cotton** and **sisal**.
Cotton grows mostly at **Alighider** in Gash-Barka. Other cotton areas: Felket and Naro.

cards.title: Dum palm (Arcobcobay)
body: Dum palm is a fibre crop that grows naturally along the **Barka and Gash** rivers.
It also grows in the south of Southern Red Sea Region: Harseile River, Simoti, Wade and Beilul.
It is **drought-resistant**. It likes flooded rivers and loose alluvial soil.
Uses: fruit (**Akat**), **buttons**, **alcohol** extraction by breweries, and fibre for **baskets**.

cards.title: Stimulant crops
body: Stimulant crops have substances that **stimulate the nervous system**: coffee, tobacco, tea.
Tobacco grows in many places but in small amounts.

cards.title: Problems of crop farming
head: Problem
What happens
rows: wrong sowing rate, weeds not removed, poor land preparation
pests lower yields; farmers too poor to buy pesticides

erosion after vegetation is removed; no land for rotation and fallowing

cards.q: Which of these is an oil seed?
cards.why: Groundnut is an oil seed. Pearl millet and sorghum are cereals; lentil is a pulse.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: 80% depend on farming. Highlands: crops. Lowlands: animals. Coast: fish and salt.
Contour ploughing traps water; rotation and fallowing keep soil fertile.
Almost all cereals, oil seeds and pulses grow in the highlands, except pearl millet and sesame.
Commercial farms: Alighider, Elabered, Sawa, Afhimbol.

cards.title: What are livestock?
body: **Livestock** are domesticated animals kept for food, draft, fibre, hides, ploughing and more.
In Eritrea: cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, horses, mules and donkeys.

cards.title: Why livestock matter
body: Animals are a source of **labour**: oxen and camels plough.
They are a source of **money and food**. Rural people sell eggs and hens to town people.
Selling livestock and products (**hides, milk, butter**) is important for the local and national economy.

cards.title: Highlands and lowlands
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Highlands
states.text: About **40%** of livestock. Land is short, so **cereal straw** is added to grazing. Villages have **communal grazing** areas; **oxen** come first.

states.label: Lowlands
states.text: About **60%** of livestock, used for **milk**. Herds **move** to find pasture and water. Camels and oxen carry goods; camels also plough.

cards.title: Problems of livestock rearing
body: **1. Diseases**: rinderpest, foot and mouth disease, anthrax, sheep pox, tuberculosis.
**2. Shortage of forage**: lowland grazing land becomes vegetable and fruit farms; in the highlands, population growth leaves little grazing land.

cards.q: Where are most of Eritrea's livestock?
cards.why: About 60% of the livestock are in the lowlands; about 40% are in the highlands.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: 40% highlands, 60% lowlands.
Problems: diseases and shortage of forage.

cards.title: A rich sea
body: The coast and islands are rich in **sea grass, sea weed, corals and mangrove forests**. These are the main **habitats** of marine animals.
So the Eritrean Red Sea is rich in **fish diversity**.
South of Massawa, **fishing** is the main activity of coastal and island people. Fish is also an important **export**.

cards.title: Why fish is important
head: Importance
rows: tasty, soft, easy to digest; rich in protein and minerals; its fat gives energy
made into glues, oils and fertilizers
liver oil, rich in vitamins A and D
foreign exchange; exported to Europe, the Middle East and the Far East

cards.title: Where fish live
body: Fish live in mangroves, salt marshes, coral reefs, sea grass beds and sandy bottoms on the shallow **continental shelf**.
The **Dahlak Archipelago** and the islands of **Hawakil Bay** are famous for **high fish diversity**.
After independence, fish were put into many new **dams**. Fishing in these lakes has started.

cards.title: Fish and salt map
body: Tap the dots. White square: rock salt.

cards.title: Salt mining
body: The Red Sea is an important source of **salt**.
**Sea salt**: made by **evaporating** sea water in many coastal areas; also at **Lake Bordele** in the Buri Peninsula.
**Rock salt**: found at **Collullui** in the Denakil Depression.

cards.title: Other marine animals
body: Besides fish, the sea has **whales, dolphins, dugong, turtles** and many birds.
Dugong, turtle and whale are **not fish**.

cards.q: Which area is famous for very high fish diversity?
cards.why: The Dahlak Archipelago, surrounded by coral reef, sea grass and sandy bottoms, is famous for its high fish diversity.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Habitats: sea grass, sea weed, corals, mangroves.
Dahlak and Hawakil: high fish diversity.
Sea salt (evaporation, Lake Bordele) and rock salt (Collullui).

cards.title: What is trade?
body: **Trade** is the exchange of **commodities** (goods) among people.
It happens between town and rural people, inside towns, and between countries.

cards.title: Kinds of trade
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Barter
states.text: **Barter** is the earliest trade: one article for another of **equal value**. Example: 1 cow for 10 sheep. It is still used in remote rural areas.

states.label: Wholesale
states.text: **Wholesale**: factories or importers sell **large amounts** to individuals, who sell to shopkeepers.

states.label: Retail
states.text: **Retail**: a shopkeeper sells goods like coffee, sugar and tea to individual customers, in **small** amounts.

cards.title: Internal (domestic) trade
body: **Internal trade** is exchange of goods **inside one country**.
In towns people buy and sell vegetables, fruits, coffee, clothes, sugar, kerosene.
Rural people sell fruits, vegetables, crops, butter, eggs and animals in towns. They buy clothes, sugar, coffee and food oil made in factories.

cards.title: International trade
body: **International trade** is trade **among countries**.
Tropical climates grow tea, coffee, tobacco, cotton, sisal, cocoa. Temperate climates grow wheat, barley, potatoes. This **regional specialization** leads to trade.
Industrialized countries export cars, airplanes, tractors, medicine and clothes. Most developing countries export farm products.

cards.q: Trade between Tessenei and Kassala (in the Sudan) is:
cards.why: Tessenei is in Eritrea and Kassala is in the Sudan. Trade among different countries is international trade.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Barter = goods for goods. Retail = small, to customers. Wholesale = large amounts.
Internal = one country. International = among countries.

cards.title: What is an industry?
body: An **industry** is a company that produces similar products.
Industries change natural resources (**raw materials**) into useful products.
Asmara Textile Industry makes **clothes** from **cotton**. Asmara Brewery makes **beer** from **barley** and some chemicals.

cards.title: Memory trick: manu + facere
body: **Manufacture** = "make by hand" (think of a **man**icure for the hands). Today it means making articles by **machinery or hand**.

cards.title: Cottage industries
body: The traditional industries are **cottage industries**: making things at **home**. They are in almost all villages.
Examples: wood carving, pottery, jewellery, basketry, weaving, metal work (goldsmith, blacksmith).
Products: ploughs, pots, clothes, bags, mats, ropes, baskets, knives, sickles, axes, shields, spears, combs, stools, earrings, necklaces, rings.

cards.title: Raw materials from nearby
body: Clay for pots and bowls. Palm leaves or bamboo for baskets. Sisal for ropes.
Workers collect raw materials from their surroundings. They sell their products and **pay tax**, which helps the local government.

cards.title: Modern industries
body: Modern manufacturing began with **Italian colonialism**.
Examples: Asmara Textile, Asmara Brewery, the Cement Factory in **Massawa** and the Refinery in **Assab**.
Also: flour and biscuit factory in **Dekemhare**, shoe factories in Asmara and Mendefera, plastic and mineral water factories.

cards.title: Industry in numbers (2003)
body: About **2241** manufacturing industries, with over **100,000** employees.
Women were about **47%** of all workers in manufacturing.
The largest industries are in **Asmara, Massawa, Assab, Dekemhare and Dubarwa**.

cards.title: Industries by region
body: Which bar is which region? Tap the dots to check. 71% are in the Central Region!

cards.q: Most modern industries in Eritrea are found in:
cards.why: 71% of all manufacturing industries are in the Central Region.

cards.title: Remember this!
body: Cottage (traditional, at home) vs modern (factories, from Italian times).
Textile ← cotton; brewery ← barley.
71% of industries in Central Region; 47% of workers are women (2003).
